title: The Faster Checkout
passage:
Imagine a supermarket replacing staffed checkouts with machines. Each machine processes a payment faster, and the manager's report records a reduction in paid staff hours. Customers now scan and pack their purchases, while one employee moves between several machines to approve sales or resolve errors.

For shoppers with a few familiar items, the arrangement may work smoothly. Someone buying loose vegetables or struggling to read the screen may take longer. A payment lasting ten seconds can follow several minutes spent entering product details or waiting for assistance.

The machines may still be worthwhile. The report includes transaction speed and staffing costs, but customers receive no wages for scanning shopping or correcting mistakes. At closing time, the manager can total the hours employees have worked. The minutes contributed by shoppers leave no equivalent entry in the accounts.
question: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage as a whole?
correct: Efficiency gains depend on whose time and effort are counted.
wrong1: Automation improves service when customers complete transactions without staff assistance.
wrong2: Faster transactions matter more to customers than individual staff support.
wrong3: Successful automation depends on giving customers less responsibility during transactions.
explanation: The report records "paid staff hours", while the "minutes contributed by shoppers" go uncounted. The apparent gain therefore depends on whose contribution is measured.
source: Original discursive text using a hypothetical supermarket. No actual company, measured efficiency gain or study result is claimed.

title: The Unfinished Wildlife Map
passage:
A wildlife map with hundreds of marked sightings can appear more informative than a mostly blank one. Suppose, however, that the first area has a popular footpath and a local recording group, while the second is difficult to reach. The same species might attract very different numbers of reports in these locations.

Inviting more volunteers could add useful records, particularly for easily recognised species. It might also multiply reports from places already well visited. Ten observations beside a car park need not describe the wildlife of a whole valley.

Researchers could investigate less accessible ground or compare records gathered with similar effort. The original map would remain valuable: it could show where a species had been seen. A blank patch would still leave several possibilities open, including an absence of animals, an absence of observers, or both.
question: Which statement best captures the central argument of the passage?
correct: Recorded patterns reflect observation methods as well as animal distribution.
wrong1: Increasing volunteer numbers makes wildlife maps more geographically representative overall.
wrong2: Reliable wildlife surveys depend chiefly on avoiding heavily visited locations.
wrong3: Unrecorded areas deserve priority because they contain more undiscovered wildlife.
explanation: The passage connects numerous reports with "a popular footpath" and allows that a blank patch could reflect "an absence of observers". The map records observation activity as well as the presence of wildlife.
source: Original discursive text using hypothetical recording conditions to explore sampling and interpretation. No actual survey, species count or research finding is reported.

title: An Opinion on Record
passage:
Public discussions leave a trail of confident statements. A speaker who repeats the same view for years can seem dependable; someone whose earlier comments conflict with later ones may face an embarrassing collection of quotations.

Those quotations can conceal different histories. One person might adopt whichever position receives the warmest applause. Another might revise a prediction after discovering that the figures behind it were incomplete. The words have changed in both cases, but the events between the statements differ.

An unchanged opinion has its own possible histories. Perhaps repeated checks have supported it; perhaps its owner has stopped checking. A recording preserves what was said, not every reason for saying it. Judging the speaker from two short clips would be convenient, especially when the original material and subsequent evidence take longer to examine.
question: What overall judgement does the passage invite the reader to make?
correct: Reliable judgement involves examining evidence behind both consistency and change.
wrong1: Consistency over time offers the strongest evidence of dependable judgement.
wrong2: Public criticism encourages speakers to replace evidence with popular opinion.
wrong3: Earlier statements deserve less weight once speakers explain their revisions.
explanation: An unchanged view could follow "repeated checks" or mean its owner has "stopped checking", while a revised view could follow applause or new figures. Consistency alone cannot distinguish these different reasons.
source: Original discursive text. The contrasting speakers are hypothetical examples, not claims about identified people or the results of a psychological study.

title: Practising Freedom
passage:
An inexperienced musician may hear a scale as a row of notes to be survived before the interesting work begins. A familiar pattern played repeatedly seems a poor preparation for producing something nobody has heard before.

Consider what happens when a performer knows an instrument well enough to move between notes without searching for them. Attention can shift towards phrasing, silence and unexpected combinations. The rehearsed movements remain, even when the resulting performance sounds spontaneous.

Practice can also become a refuge. A player may perfect increasingly difficult exercises while postponing the uncertain business of making musical choices. Fluent fingers do not decide which phrase deserves to be heard. A listener encounters the performance, not the hours behind it, and two equally accomplished players may produce music with very different effects.
question: Which statement best expresses the argument developed across the passage?
correct: Technical discipline can enable originality without determining its artistic value.
wrong1: Technical fluency matters chiefly when performers reproduce familiar musical patterns.
wrong2: Spontaneous performances succeed when musicians stop relying on rehearsed movements.
wrong3: Musical practice contributes more to accuracy than to expressive possibilities.
explanation: Familiar movements allow attention to shift towards "unexpected combinations", but "Fluent fingers do not decide which phrase deserves to be heard." Practice creates possibilities without settling their artistic worth.
source: Original discursive arts commentary using illustrative musicians. No specific performance or empirical research result is claimed.

title: The Quiet Repair
passage:
After several winters without flooding, a town's drainage team may struggle to explain why its maintenance budget is still needed. The most noticeable part of its work is often a temporary road closure. A photograph of workers clearing a blocked channel shows disruption; a photograph taken weeks later may show an ordinary dry street.

That dry street does not, by itself, establish what the workers achieved. Perhaps the season brought little rain. Perhaps the water would have drained away without intervention. Records of rainfall, blockages and previous flooding would give the picture more meaning.

Emergency repairs produce different evidence: damaged property can be photographed, and progress is visible as water recedes. Routine maintenance offers fewer dramatic comparisons. A report built around easily photographed changes could give these two kinds of work very different prominence.
question: Which conclusion takes account of the whole passage?
correct: Assessing prevention requires evidence beyond whether a visible crisis occurred.
wrong1: Preventive maintenance deserves support whenever disruption produces no visible damage.
wrong2: Emergency repairs provide stronger evidence of value than routine maintenance.
wrong3: Public support for maintenance depends mainly on reducing temporary disruption.
explanation: The dry street could reflect successful maintenance, but "Perhaps the season brought little rain." Routine work also offers "fewer dramatic comparisons", so its value requires evidence beyond visible events.
source: Original discursive text using a hypothetical town and maintenance team. No actual flood history, spending figure or engineering assessment is reported.
